question: On SQL Server Express, which memory consumer does the edition's memory cap apply to, and does its CPU limit count sockets or cores?
answer: The cap applies only to the buffer pool (other caches can grow up to max server memory); the CPU limit is one socket, not one CPU, so multiple cores on that socket are used.
support: The 1GB limit is only for the buffer pool | SQL Express enforces one socket, not one CPU

question: On Ubuntu, where does ISC dhcpd keep its lease database, and what timezone are the timestamps in that file recorded in?
answer: /var/lib/dhcp/dhcpd.leases on Ubuntu; all times in the file are in UTC (GMT), not local time.
support: On Ubuntu there is the file /var/lib/dhcp/dhcpd.leases | All times in this file are in UTC (GMT), not your local timezone.

question: Which pipeline prints only the grand total disk usage of a set of *.sql files, and which one lists directories sorted by size, largest first, in human-readable units?
answer: du -c -- *.sql | tail -n 1 gives the total; du -sh -- */ | sort -rh lists directories largest first (GNU sort and du).

question: Which gcc options produce annotated assembly to read when learning how code maps to machine instructions, and why are CPU opcode values not chosen arbitrarily?
answer: gcc -S -O2 -fverbose-asm outputs readable assembly; opcodes are chosen so groups of bits enable or disable logic gates in the ALU, which reduces ALU complexity.
support: Reading the assembly code (generated by gcc -S -O2 -fverbose-asm) can also be helpful. | Well-chosen opcodes reduce the complexity of the ALU.

question: How do I find which kernel release contains a given fix using the kernel.org git web interface, and what does GitHub's kernel repository offer to see more tags for a commit?
answer: On git web, click commitdiff, then raw, and read the X-Git-Tag header; on GitHub, click the three dots to see the full list of tags/kernel versions.
support: look at the X-Git-Tag header | If three-dots are clicked, full list of tags/kernel versions can be seen.

question: Why does GNU tr mangle UTF-8 characters, and what must a Perl one-liner add so tr/// with fullwidth letters in its source code works, given that -C alone does not help?
answer: GNU tr doesn't support multi-byte characters; in Perl add use utf8 (or -Mutf8) so the source is read as UTF-8, because -C only controls IO.
support: but that it doesn't support multi-byte characters | You need to use utf8 to have your Perl (5) source itself encoded in that way

question: In an interactive shell, why does foo=hello echo $foo print nothing, and what sequence of commands is a one-command prefix assignment functionally equivalent to?
answer: The shell expands $foo before running the command, when it is not yet set; prefix assignment equals export TEST=foo, running the application, then unset TEST.
support: The shell will expand the variable before running the command | The shell syntax describes this as being functionally equivalent to

question: Where should an SSD partition start to get roughly 70 MB/s writes instead of 29 MB/s, and in which kernel version did the log-structured NILFS2 filesystem become available?
answer: Starting the partition at sector 128 gave 70MB/s versus 29MB/s with default alignment from sector 63; NILFS2 became available in kernel 2.6.30.
support: vs 70MB/s with proper alignment [ starting from 128rd sector ] | will be available in kernel 2.6.30

question: Why is web search a poor way to discover concepts you do not yet know exist, and what do Q&A sites add that makes them a complement to programming books?
answer: Search helps with how to do something but not with finding what you don't know; Q&A sites add interaction, letting you ask questions a book leaves unanswered, so they complement books.
support: Google is great to find out how to do something, but it's not great for finding out what you don't know | No, it is not a substitute, but a perfect complement.

question: Why might a btrfs balance with conversion filters have no effect on a 4.0 kernel, and which command cleans up leftover single chunks that have zero usage?
answer: A kernel 4.0 regression made conversion filters in balance have no effect; clean up empty single chunks with btrfs balance start -dusage=0 -musage=0 on the mount point.
support: This is a regression in kernel 4.0, causing conversion filters in balance to have no effect | btrfs balance start -dusage=0 -musage=0 /mnt/btrfs

question: In SQL Server, what permission benefit is lost by spreading related code across separate databases, and what kind of data requirement forces tables to share one database?
answer: Ownership chaining is lost, so the login needs permissions on objects in both databases; data needing transactional and referential consistency must live in the same database.
support: However, you lose ownership chaining like this. | Data that needs to be transactionally and referentially consistent needs to be in the same database.

question: Which ufw file holds NAT port-forward rules, and which commands remove them again?
answer: Add a *nat PREROUTING REDIRECT block to /etc/ufw/before.rules; to cancel, run ufw disable, iptables --table nat --flush, iptables --table nat --delete-chain, then ufw enable.
support: Add the lines below to /etc/ufw/before.rules | iptables --table nat --flush

question: Why does piping grep into xargs dirname inside find -exec print a usage message for files that don't match, and how can bash make a shell function available to find -exec?
answer: When grep matches nothing, xargs runs dirname with no arguments; for functions, run export -f foo and use find ... -exec bash -c 'foo "$@"' bash {} +.
support: xargs launches dirname without any arguments | bash allows one to export functions via the environment with export -f

question: When unit testing an abstract C++ class, what should the tests verify, and which pattern lets the same tests run against every concrete subclass?
answer: Test behavior (what func returns or how it changes state), not implementation; use the Abstract Test pattern: an abstract base test class with a factory method, plus one derived test class per subclass.
support: What you are actually testing now is implementation, and not the behavior. | NUnit (and I believe JUnit) let you implement the Abstract Test pattern.

question: Which license exception covers binaries compiled with GCC, and what is the one thing the GPL actually restricts regarding the compiler itself?
answer: The GCC Runtime Library Exception; the restriction is modifying the GNU compiler itself and not releasing those modifications under the GPL.
support: This would be covered by the GCC Runtime Library Exception. | What you are restricted from is modifying the GNU compiler itself and not putting those modifications under the GPL.

question: Why do exported variables from a shell script vanish after I run it, and what file permission difference is there between running it directly and passing its path to an interpreter?
answer: Executing runs it in a subshell, so exports vanish (source it with . env.sh instead); running directly needs the executable bit, while passing the path to an interpreter does not.
support: When you execute the script, it is run in a subshell | the script must be marked executable to run it directly, but not to run it by passing the path to the interpreter

question: How can a batch file wait 5 seconds using choice, and what switch makes timeout ignore key presses?
answer: choice /d y /t 5 > nul waits 5 seconds; timeout /t N /nobreak ignores key presses except an explicit CTRL-C.
support: choice /d y /t 5 > nul | the command also accepts the optional switch /nobreak

question: When installing a self-contained package under /opt, where is its executable symlinked, and what per-user alternative uses a single directory in PATH filled with symlinks?
answer: Symlink the executable into /usr/bin; the per-user alternative is a single directory such as ~/bin in PATH with symbolic links created there (e.g. with Stow).
support: sym-link the executable back to /usr/bin | put a single directory such as ~/bin in your PATH, and when you install software, create symbolic links in ~/bin

question: Why does a for loop sent over ssh in double quotes expand variables on the local machine, and what can you do when the remote login shell is tcsh?
answer: The local shell expands variables inside double quotes, so use single quotes; with a tcsh login shell, start sh explicitly (sh -c) or run a script via ssh host sh ./script.sh.
support: Simply use single quotes (') instead and your problem will disappear | you may want to explicitly start a sh shell
